title: Pharmacologic and Non‑pharmacologic Management of COPD Exacerbations
summary: Evidence-based, stepwise management of acute COPD exacerbations with integration of adjunctive non‑pharmacologic strategies to improve outcomes and reduce recurrence risk.
clinicalQuestion: What are the optimal pharmacologic and non‑pharmacologic interventions for managing acute COPD exacerbations and preventing future events?

heroStats.label: Adherence impact
heroStats.value: Poor inhaler adherence ↑ exacerbation risk by **40% (RR ≈1.40)** [1]

heroStats.label: Antibiotic stewardship
heroStats.value: PCT guidance ↓ antibiotic exposure by **~2.0 days (p=0.04)** without worse outcomes [2]

heroStats.label: CV risk window
heroStats.value: Exacerbations linked to ↑ near‑term cardiovascular events post‑AECOPD [3], [4]

keyMoments.title: Triage early and treat hypoxemia
keyMoments.body: Assess work of breathing, mental status, hemodynamics; give controlled oxygen to target SpO2 88–92% and escalate ventilatory support as needed [5].

keyMoments.title: Initiate core pharmacotherapy
keyMoments.body: Short‑acting bronchodilators, systemic steroids (short course), and antibiotics when bacterial features or moderate–severe exacerbation are present [6], [7].

keyMoments.title: Steward antibiotics with PCT
keyMoments.body: Use procalcitonin to reduce unnecessary antibiotic days without harming clinical outcomes [2].

keyMoments.title: Start early mobilization and PR
keyMoments.body: Begin in-hospital exercise and arrange pulmonary rehabilitation promptly to limit functional decline [5].

keyMoments.title: Plan for prevention at discharge
keyMoments.body: Optimize long‑term inhaled therapy, vaccination, adherence, and CV risk mitigation; schedule follow‑up within 2–4 weeks [6], [3], [1].

sections.title: Stepwise Management of the Acute Exacerbation
sections.blurb: A concise, evidence‑anchored sequence for ED/inpatient care.

steps.title: Assess severity and stabilize
steps.body: Evaluate ABCs, mental status, and signs of hypercapnia. Provide controlled oxygen to SpO2 88–92%. Consider non‑invasive ventilation for hypercapnic acidosis or increased work of breathing; escalate if failing. Nonpharmacologic respiratory support is a core component of acute care [5].

steps.title: Bronchodilation
steps.body: Administer short‑acting beta‑agonist (albuterol) ± short‑acting muscarinic antagonist (ipratropium) via MDI with spacer or nebulizer at frequent intervals, then titrate to response. Combination SABA+SAMA provides additive bronchodilation during AECOPD [6], [7].

steps.title: Systemic corticosteroids
steps.body: Give a short course to hasten recovery and reduce treatment failure; typical regimen is prednisone 40 mg PO daily for 5 days (or IV methylprednisolone if oral not feasible). Keep course short to minimize adverse effects while achieving benefit [6], [7].

steps.title: Antibiotics when indicated
steps.body: Indications include increased dyspnea, sputum volume, and sputum purulence; need for ventilatory support; or clinical suspicion of bacterial infection. Choose local‑guided agents targeting H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae, M. catarrhalis, and, in severe disease or risk factors, Pseudomonas. Consider **procalcitonin‑guided** decisions to safely reduce exposure by **~2 days (p=0.04)** [2].

steps.title: Adjuncts and comorbidity vigilance
steps.body: Continue long‑acting inhalers as feasible; avoid routine methylxanthines due to toxicity. Monitor for arrhythmias, heart failure, and acute coronary syndromes; AECOPD confers **elevated short‑term CV risk** requiring proactive mitigation and surveillance [3], [4].

sections.title: Non‑pharmacologic Interventions
sections.blurb: Integrate throughout admission and transition of care to reduce disability and recurrence.

cards.title: Pulmonary Rehabilitation & Exercise
items: Early in‑hospital mobilization reduces functional decline and supports recovery; arrange PR promptly post‑discharge [5].
PR improves exercise capacity and health status; embed within comprehensive COPD care pathways [8], [5].

cards.title: Oxygen Strategy
items: Target SpO2 88–92% to avoid CO2 narcosis; reassess ABGs after initiation [5].
Evaluate for long‑term oxygen therapy post‑stabilization if persistent severe hypoxemia is present [6].

cards.title: Education, Adherence, and Inhaler Technique
items: Teach inhaler technique and provide device selection aligned with patient ability; reinforce before discharge [6].
Address adherence: poor adherence increases exacerbation risk by **~40% (RR ≈1.40)** [1].

cards.title: Cardiovascular Risk Mitigation
items: Screen for ischemia, arrhythmia, and heart failure during AECOPD; risk is heightened post‑event [3], [4].
Optimize statins, antiplatelets, BP control, and smoking cessation per primary prevention frameworks [3], [4].

cards.title: Antibiotic Stewardship
items: Use PCT and clinical features to guide initiation/discontinuation; PCT guidance reduces exposure without worsening outcomes [2].
Reassess at 48–72 hours; de‑escalate or stop if bacterial infection unlikely [2].

cards.title: Follow‑up and Care Transitions
items: Schedule follow‑up within 2–4 weeks to reassess symptoms, spirometry as appropriate, and inhaler regimen [6].
Refer to PR, ensure vaccinations, and finalize an individualized action plan [8], [6].

sections.title: Preventing Future Exacerbations After Recovery
sections.blurb: Consolidate long‑term strategies shown to reduce exacerbation frequency and improve quality of life.

cards.title: Optimize Inhaled Therapy
items: Escalate to dual or triple therapy (LABA/LAMA ± ICS) based on exacerbation history and eosinophil count; goal is symptom control and exacerbation reduction [6], [9].
Reassess need for ICS in low eosinophil counts due to pneumonia risk; maintain if frequent exacerbations and eosinophils elevated [6].

cards.title: Lifestyle and Risk Factor Modification
items: Smoking cessation, vaccinations (influenza, pneumococcal, COVID‑19), weight and nutrition optimization, and activity promotion [8], [6].
Home action plans and rescue packs when appropriate; ensure clear instructions to avoid overtreatment [8], [6].

cards.title: Comorbidity Integration
items: Screen for and treat anxiety/depression, osteoporosis, GERD, and CV disease; these impact exacerbation risk and recovery [10], [3].
Coordinate primary care and cardiology follow‑up given post‑AECOPD CV risk signal [3], [4].
